slides.0.title: Course Introduction
slides.0.content:
Most people think of Napa and Sonoma first, yet California has 154 AVAs (per the TTB list and Capstone; the number keeps growing), many of them inland or in the south. This lesson fills gaps from Level 1: Lodi and its 7 sub-AVAs, the Sacramento Valley, the San Joaquin Valley and Southern California.

Learning Objectives

🌾 Read Lodi's sub-AVAs

Name the 7 Lodi sub-AVAs and understand the Tokay, San Joaquin and Redding soil series

🌊 Know the Sacramento Valley AVAs

Clarksburg, Suisun Valley, Solano County Green Valley, Capay Valley and Dunnigan Hills

⛰️ Read the San Joaquin Valley's fringe AVAs

Madera, Tracy Hills, Diablo Grande, Salado Creek, Squaw Valley–Miramonte, Tehachapi Mountains

🌴 Grasp Southern California's sea-breeze logic

South Coast AVA and the Temecula, Ramona and San Pasqual AVAs inside it, plus Malibu Coast and Cucamonga Valley

📌 Source note: AVA names and counties follow the TTB; area and production figures are not used because the source pages contain contradictory numbers.
slides.1.title: Lodi & the Delta: 7 Sub-AVAs
slides.1.content:
🌾 Lodi AVA (established 1986) and its 7 sub-AVAs

Lodi AVA was established in 1986 across Sacramento and San Joaquin Counties. Capstone cites roughly 100,000 acres of vines; the climate is Mediterranean, and low-lying sub-AVAs in the Delta area (such as Cosumnes River) are cooled by fog. From 2006 (per Capstone) seven sub-AVAs were carved out (TTB: 27 CFR 9.195–9.201):

Alta Mesa

Sacramento County (TTB). Capstone describes a 'high table' plateau with shallow San Joaquin series sandy clay loam over clay and sandstone hardpan; low elevation (about 10–41 m).

Borden Ranch

Sacramento and San Joaquin Counties (TTB). Named for Borden Ranch; Redding series rocky clay loam; elevation about 22–158 m (Capstone).

Clements Hills

San Joaquin County (TTB). Redding series rocky clay loam; Capstone calls it the sub-AVA with Lodi's widest diurnal swing.

Cosumnes River

Sacramento County (TTB). Near sea level, influenced by Delta fog, so one of the cooler sub-AVAs; San Joaquin series soils.

Jahant

Sacramento and San Joaquin Counties (TTB). Named for the Jahant family; Capstone calls it one of Lodi's cooler sub-AVAs.

Mokelumne River

San Joaquin County (TTB). Mainly deep Tokay series fine sandy loam; Capstone calls it the sub-AVA with the most vineyard area and among the cooler ones.

Sloughhouse

Sacramento County (TTB). Named for Slough House; Redding series soils; Capstone calls it Lodi's warmest.

Variety profile (Capstone, 2019 plantings)

About 71% red and 29% white; leading varieties are Cabernet Sauvignon, Zinfandel, Chardonnay, Merlot, Pinot Gris and Petite Sirah. Lodi is known both for old-vine Zinfandel and for recent plantings of Portuguese and Italian varieties.

⚠️ Study note: Capstone's 'largest/smallest' statements are not consistent within its own pages. For exams, focus on the 7 sub-AVA names and the three soil series: Tokay, San Joaquin, Redding.
slides.2.title: Sacramento Valley: Delta Breezes and the AVAs of Solano and Yolo
slides.2.content:
🌊 AVAs of the Sacramento Valley

Soils are mostly alluvial topsoil over sedimentary subsoil; most of the valley is Winkler-Amerine Region IV–V, with Region III near the bay (Capstone). The key question is whether Delta and bay breezes reach the vines.

Clarksburg

Spans Sacramento, Solano and Yolo Counties (TTB). A near-sea-level Delta plain with poorly drained clay and clay loam and a high water table; Capstone lists Chenin Blanc, Chardonnay and Petite Sirah, Region III. Merritt Island is nested inside it.

Suisun Valley

Solano County (TTB). Warm-summer Mediterranean climate; Capstone notes at least 24 varieties, with an emphasis on Petite Sirah.

Solano County Green Valley

Solano County (TTB). East of Napa, often foggy and cooler; Capstone lists Petite Sirah, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Merlot and Syrah. Do not confuse it with Sonoma's Green Valley of Russian River Valley.

Capay Valley

Yolo County (TTB). Northeast of Lake Berryessa and east of the Vaca Range, with hot summers; Capstone lists Tempranillo, Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Grenache, Viognier and others.

Dunnigan Hills

Yolo County (TTB). Rolling hills about 30 miles northwest of Sacramento (Capstone) with well-drained gravelly loams; irrigation needed, cooler than the valley floor; Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Tempranillo, Syrah, Chardonnay.

North Yuba

Yuba County (TTB), inside the Sierra Foothills AVA. Capstone calls it 'Yuba': decomposed granite, quartz and volcanic rock; varieties include Cabernet Sauvignon and Pinot Noir.

📌 Compare: Solano County Green Valley is in Solano County; Sonoma's is formally Green Valley of Russian River Valley — a different AVA.
slides.3.title: San Joaquin Valley: Fringe AVAs from Valley Floor to Foothills
slides.3.content:
⛰️ AVAs of the San Joaquin Valley (Capstone supplement)

The San Joaquin Valley is one of California's largest grape-growing areas, mostly for bulk wine, yet it holds several small AVAs. Most sit on the valley's edge or in the foothills, using elevation, wind and soil for differentiation.

Madera

Fresno and Madera Counties (TTB). Winkler-Amerine Region V, irrigated; Capstone lists French Colombard, Chardonnay, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Zinfandel.

Tracy Hills

San Joaquin and Stanislaus Counties (TTB). Alluvial soils from the Diablo Range, some very gravelly; Capstone lists less common varieties such as Tempranillo, Sagrantino, Aglianico, Nero d'Avola and Touriga Nacional.

Diablo Grande

Stanislaus County (TTB), established 1998 (Capstone). Hilly, 244–792 m, with vines at 305–549 m.

Salado Creek

Stanislaus County (TTB), approved 2004 (Capstone). Ensalado series soil; Capstone notes no wine was then labelled with this AVA.

River Junction

San Joaquin County (TTB), in the Delta area; Capstone's page does not name this AVA, so only its name and county from the TTB are given here.

Squaw Valley–Miramonte

Fresno County (TTB), established 2015 (Capstone). Foothills with decomposed granite, 488–1,067 m; a higher, cooler mountain setting.

Tehachapi Mountains

Kern County (TTB). 1,097–1,646 m, little rain mostly in winter (Capstone); Winkler-Amerine Region II, borderline III.

⚠️ Study note: Capstone has obvious typos in Diablo Grande's area and the River Junction heading, so area and production figures are not used.
slides.4.title: Southern California: Sea Breezes, Granite and the South Coast AVA
slides.4.content:
🌴 The logic of Southern California

Sun is strong and rain scarce; cooling comes from sea air funnelled through mountain gaps and from cold air sinking at night. South Coast AVA (TTB: Orange, Riverside, San Bernardino and San Diego Counties) is the large umbrella AVA; Capstone says it fully includes Ramona Valley, San Pasqual Valley and Temecula Valley.

Temecula Valley

Riverside County (TTB). About 22 miles from the coast; marine air mainly enters via the Santa Margarita Gap, with the Rainbow Gap a lesser route; vineyards sit on 1,200–1,600 ft benchlands with well-drained decomposed-granite sandy loams (Capstone). Varieties include Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Petite Sirah, Viognier and Vermentino.

Ramona Valley

San Diego County (TTB). About 25 miles from the Pacific; Capstone gives Winkler Region III and well-drained sandy loams; viticulture is practical up to about 2,640 ft.

San Pasqual Valley

San Diego County (TTB). Between Escondido and Ramona at roughly 300–500 ft on alluvial soils; growing-season highs rarely exceed 95°F (Capstone).

Malibu Coast

Los Angeles and Ventura Counties (TTB). A coastal foothill AVA separate from South Coast (covered in Level 1).

Cucamonga Valley

Riverside and San Bernardino Counties (TTB). Only the name and counties are confirmed from the TTB here; Capstone's page could not be retrieved, so no further details are given.

⚠️ Study note: Capstone's San Diego County page is inconsistent in °F/°C diurnal-range conversions, so no diurnal figures are used.
